One of its most prolific subfields is that of Music Generation (also called Algorithmic Composition or Musical Metacreation), that uses computational means to compose music. Due to the multidisciplinary nature of this research field, it is sometimes hard to define precise goals and to keep track of what problems can be considered solved by state-of-the-art systems and what instead needs further developments. With this survey, we try to give a complete introduction to those who wish to explore Computational Creativity and Music Generation. To do so, we first give a picture of the research on the definition and the evaluation of creativity, both human and computational, needed to understand how computational means can be used to obtain creative behaviors and its importance within Artificial Intelligence studies. We then review the state of the art of Music Generation Systems, by citing examples for all the main approaches to music generation, and by listing the open challenges that were identified by previous reviews on the subject. However, R&D teams may also have autonomy in choosing which problems to address (strategic autonomy), the effects of which remain underexplored. This study examines how strategic autonomy influences the cognitive process of problem representation and in turn, the creativity of inventions produced by R&D teams. Leveraging a unique dataset consisting of descriptions of problems in invention disclosures by R&D professionals of a firm, along with information on whether an invention was autonomously initiated, we find that problem representation complexity is lower for autonomous inventions, or inventions for which R&D teams exert strategic autonomy to identify problems themselves, than top-down inventions for which problems are identified and assigned to them by managers. We further find that domain expertise and multi-project engagement of team members moderate this relationship, and that lower problem representation complexity in turn relates to lower creativity of inventions. By uncovering a novel mechanism through which autonomy negatively affects creativity, this study contributes to the literatures on creativity, innovation, and organizational design.\"}, {\"id\": {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=active+inference+epistemic+curiosity+exploration+autonomous+agent+problem+selection&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.1007/s10458-025-09702-y\", \"title\": [\"Correction: Epistemic selection of costly alternatives: the case of participatory budgeting\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/s10458-025-09702-y\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 4, 29]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/springerreference_301925\", \"title\": [\"Epistemic Curiosity\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/springerreference_301925\"}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/s10458-024-09683-4\", \"title\": [\"Information gathering in POMDPs using active inference\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/s10458-024-09683-4\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2024, 11, 7]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.31234/osf.io/tqf9s_v1\", \"title\": [\"Contextually Attuned Understanding of Epistemic Curiosity in Early Childhood: An Emic Exploration in Nepal\"], \"abstract\": \"

Child-centered and play-based education interventions, increasingly adopted worldwide, often aim to foster epistemic curiosity – the desire for new information – to enhance children’s learning. Dominant Western frameworks conceptualize curiosity as expressed through independent exploration and proactive questioning, treating these behaviors as prototypical indicators of curiosity. However, this characterization is largely derived from research in high-income Western contexts, raising concerns about its cross-cultural validity in non-Western low- and middle-income countries. This qualitative study examines how epistemic curiosity is expressed and interpreted in early childhood classrooms in Nepal. We analyzed data from focus groups with parents and child development experts, interviews with teachers, and classroom observations. Findings revealed expressions of curiosity that extend beyond Western prototypes, particularly attentive information-seeking, such as focused listening. These attentive behaviors were socially valued because they aligned with relational norms emphasizing respect and harmony. By conceptualizing curiosity as a universal construct with context-adaptive manifestations shaped by cultural and sociodemographic dynamics, this study advances a more inclusive framework for studying curiosity across diverse contexts. It challenges indicators that privilege independence and psychological autonomy as the primary expressions of curiosity. This study also highlights auxiliary skills that operate alongside curiosity and variation in adults’ perceptions across demographic contexts.
